title: Singapore Oceanarium Animals
summary: Travel from ancient waters and Singapore's coast to coral reefs, open ocean and the abyss, meeting the animals officially named by Singapore Oceanarium along the way.

nodes.summary: Zoom from six ocean story zones into habitats and all 43 entries in Singapore Oceanarium's official Animals A–Z catalogue.
nodes.key_fact: The A–Z catalogue contains 43 source-checked entries, including live displays, rotating displays, preserved specimens and one clearly labelled replica.
nodes.explainer: Follow the globe from zone to habitat to animal. Every A–Z profile shows a real photograph, animal type, natural habitat, Oceanarium exhibit and natural diet. Presentation labels prevent replicas and specimens from being mistaken for live residents.
nodes.why_it_matters: Organising animals by habitat reveals more than an alphabetical list: body shapes, senses, feeding strategies and migrations make sense when you see the environments that shaped them.
nodes.wonder: If you could explore only one layer of the ocean—from mangrove mud to the abyss—which would you choose?

glossary.definition: The place and conditions in which an organism normally lives.
A group of organisms that share defining biological characteristics and can usually reproduce with one another.

nodes.summary: Meet ancient lineages and animals that illuminate the long journey from early ocean life toward life on land.
nodes.key_fact: Sea jellies have existed for more than 500 million years.
nodes.explainer: This zone uses living animals alongside fossils, replicas and digital reconstructions. The globe includes only the living animals named by the Oceanarium and clearly leaves extinct display animals out of the resident list.
nodes.why_it_matters: Living species can preserve body plans and survival strategies with very deep evolutionary histories.
nodes.wonder: Which is more surprising: an animal that barely changed, or one that found a new way to live?

nodes.summary: Explore Singapore's mangrove coast, where animals switch between water, mud, air and changing tides.
nodes.key_fact: Intertidal animals may experience wet, dry, salty, hot and cool conditions within a single day.
nodes.explainer: Mangroves and mudflats are border worlds. Their residents need ways to cling, burrow, breathe, hide or move as the tide repeatedly covers and uncovers the shore.
nodes.why_it_matters: These animals make Singapore's own marine biodiversity visible and connect coastal development to habitat protection.
nodes.wonder: What would you need to survive if your home disappeared underwater twice a day?

nodes.summary: Enter bright reefs and open water filled with sharks, rays, corals, clams, seadragons and reef fish.
nodes.key_fact: Most ocean species live in the sunlit upper ocean and shallow seas.
nodes.explainer: Sunlight powers algae and plankton, which support complex food webs. Reefs add three-dimensional shelter; open water rewards efficient swimming and wide-ranging senses.
nodes.why_it_matters: The richest-looking zone also shows how closely predators, grazers, filter feeders and habitat-building corals depend on one another.
nodes.wonder: Why might a healthy reef need both tiny filter feeders and large sharks?

nodes.summary: Follow currents, daily migrations, bottom-dwellers and animals using human-made reefs.
nodes.key_fact: Many marine animals travel vertically each day as light changes, forming the planet's largest repeated animal migration by biomass.
nodes.explainer: This zone links movement to survival: some animals drift, some school, some migrate vast distances, and others stay close to the seafloor or shelter in wrecks.
nodes.why_it_matters: Ocean currents and animal movements carry energy and nutrients between places and depths that can seem separate.
nodes.wonder: How can an animal navigate across an ocean with no road signs?

nodes.summary: Discover live deep-sea animals adapted to cold, darkness, pressure and very limited food.
nodes.key_fact: A whale carcass reaching the seafloor can feed a changing community of organisms for years or even decades.
nodes.explainer: Much of this zone uses specimens and projections because deep-sea animals are difficult to observe and care for. This globe's resident branch includes only the three live animals explicitly named for the Whale Fall and Seamount habitat.
nodes.why_it_matters: Deep habitats show that life can persist with no sunlight by using falling food, scavenging and chemosynthetic ecosystems.
nodes.wonder: How do you find food in a place that is always dark?

nodes.summary: A slow-moving world of living sea jellies, with species changing as the Oceanarium rotates displays.
nodes.key_fact: The Moon Jelly habitat holds thousands of animals in a circular-flow Kreisel system.
nodes.explainer: Sea jellies have no bones, heart or brain. Their soft bells pulse to move, while tentacles and oral arms help capture food.
nodes.why_it_matters: Their simple-looking bodies are highly successful and reveal an ancient branch of animal evolution.
nodes.wonder: How can an animal coordinate movement without a brain?

nodes.summary: Living animals with ancient evolutionary histories share the story with fossils and replicas.
nodes.key_fact: Horseshoe crab relatives existed hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs.
nodes.explainer: A lineage can be ancient even though every living individual is modern. These species are not 'unchanged fossils'; they continue to evolve while retaining recognisable ancestral features.
nodes.why_it_matters: Comparing fins, gills, lungs, armour and senses helps reconstruct major transitions in vertebrate and arthropod history.
nodes.wonder: Which body feature can tell the longest evolutionary story?

nodes.summary: Living amphibians reveal both the possibilities and vulnerabilities of a life shared between water and land.
nodes.key_fact: Amphibian skin is permeable, so water quality and moisture can affect them directly.
nodes.explainer: Amphibians link aquatic ancestry with life on land. Their eggs, larvae, skin and breathing strategies show why moving onto land required many coordinated changes.
nodes.why_it_matters: Because many amphibians respond quickly to environmental change, their decline can warn us that habitats are under stress.
nodes.wonder: What is the hardest problem an aquatic animal faces when it moves onto land?

nodes.summary: Live mangrove and intertidal residents demonstrate the ingenious ways local animals manage changing tides.
nodes.key_fact: The official habitat page names four live examples: Archerfish, Barred Mudskipper, Knobbly Sea Star and Spotted Seahorse.
nodes.explainer: The animals here use very different solutions—accurate water jets, air exposure, tube feet and grasping tails—but all depend on complex coastal habitat.
nodes.why_it_matters: Knowing nearby species turns conservation from an abstract global issue into care for Singapore's own shores.
nodes.wonder: Which adaptation would help most in a mangrove: aiming, walking, gripping or clinging?

nodes.summary: Meet sharks with different body shapes, hunting tools and reproductive strategies.
nodes.key_fact: Sharks detect faint electrical fields produced by other animals.
nodes.explainer: Sharks are cartilaginous fishes: their skeletons are built mainly from cartilage rather than bone. Different species cruise open water, rest near the bottom or use specialised heads and senses to find prey.
nodes.why_it_matters: Many shark populations recover slowly because the animals mature late and produce relatively few young.
nodes.wonder: Why might a frightening appearance tell you very little about an animal's behaviour?

nodes.summary: Corals, giant clams and moray eels reveal a reef built by animals and crowded with partnerships.
nodes.key_fact: Corals and giant clams are animals, even though they may look like rocks, plants or giant shells.
nodes.explainer: Reef-builders create shelter. Filter feeders clean particles from water. Predators use holes and crevices. Together they turn a hard structure into a living neighbourhood.
nodes.why_it_matters: When reef-building corals are damaged, many other species lose feeding, nursery and hiding places.
nodes.wonder: Can one animal be a home for hundreds of others?

nodes.summary: Camouflage, armour, venom, colour and partnerships help small and medium animals survive busy reefs.
nodes.key_fact: Reef species often depend on a precise microhabitat, such as seagrass, anemones, kelp or branching coral.
nodes.explainer: Every shape tells a story: tubes suck tiny prey, spines deter predators, leaf-like fins hide an animal, and beaks scrape food from hard surfaces.
nodes.why_it_matters: Specialisation can be very effective, but it also makes animals vulnerable when their particular habitat disappears.
nodes.wonder: Would you rather survive by hiding, warning, armouring or partnering?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — Reef Animals and Kelp Forest

nodes.summary: Large rays, sharks and fishes share the Oceanarium's broadest living seascape.
nodes.key_fact: The Oceanarium's largest viewing panel looks into this habitat.
nodes.explainer: Open-water animals often need efficient swimming, broad sensory awareness and ways to feed while covering large areas. Reef-associated giants also move between shelter and open water.
nodes.why_it_matters: Wide-ranging species connect distant habitats and can cross many human jurisdictions during their lives.
nodes.wonder: What would it feel like to live in a home with almost nowhere to hide?

nodes.summary: A drifting Sargassum community shows how a moving habitat can carry its own residents.
nodes.key_fact: Floating Sargassum can form rafts that provide food, camouflage and nursery habitat far from shore.
nodes.explainer: The current is both transport and habitat. Animals living among floating seaweed need to remain close to it, match it or feed on the tiny organisms gathered there.
nodes.why_it_matters: Currents connect ecosystems, but they also collect human debris and transport it across oceans.
nodes.wonder: How do you stay home when your entire home is drifting?

nodes.summary: One habitat follows daily vertical travellers; another follows dolphins that range horizontally through coastal seas.
nodes.key_fact: Light, food, temperature, reproduction and predators can all trigger migration.
nodes.explainer: Vertical migration changes depth, sometimes every day. Horizontal migration crosses regions or oceans. Both require animals to sense changing conditions and spend energy at the right time.
nodes.why_it_matters: Migrating animals transfer nutrients and depend on safe routes rather than a single protected place.
nodes.wonder: What invisible clues could tell an animal when and where to travel?

nodes.summary: Bottom-associated animals hunt, hide, graze and filter-feed around rock and reef.
nodes.key_fact: Benthos means organisms living on, in or near the seabed.
nodes.explainer: The seafloor provides surfaces, burrows and crevices. Its residents may be powerful crabs, secretive eels or brightly coloured reef fishes.
nodes.why_it_matters: The bottom is not empty space; it is a layered community that recycles nutrients and provides shelter.
nodes.wonder: Why might staying close to the bottom be safer than swimming in open water?

nodes.summary: Sharks and rays move through a shipwreck-inspired habitat showing how structures can become reef-like shelter.
nodes.key_fact: Wrecks and purpose-built reefs can add hard surfaces and hiding places where natural structure is limited.
nodes.explainer: Artificial reefs are not substitutes for protecting natural reefs, but carefully designed structures can provide habitat and research opportunities.
nodes.why_it_matters: The design, material, location and monitoring of an artificial habitat determine whether it helps or harms marine life.
nodes.wonder: What would you include if you designed a safe underwater neighbourhood?

nodes.summary: Three named live residents show how deep-sea animals use scarce food and survive extreme conditions.
nodes.key_fact: The live habitat names a Japanese Isopod, Deepsea Akaza Prawn and Australian Ghostshark.
nodes.explainer: Deep-sea animals may grow slowly, conserve energy and rely on scattered food. The surrounding whale-fall story shows how one large pulse of organic matter can support an entire succession of life.
nodes.why_it_matters: The deep sea is connected to surface life by sinking particles, migrating animals and falling carcasses.
nodes.wonder: How could one dead whale create many new lives?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — Whale Fall and Seamount

nodes.summary: A translucent jelly with a gently pulsing bell and four commonly visible, horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs.
nodes.key_fact: Water makes up most of a Moon Jelly's body.
nodes.explainer: The bell contracts to push water, while cilia and oral arms move captured plankton toward the mouth. A loose nerve net coordinates simple responses without a central brain.
nodes.why_it_matters: Moon Jellies make nervous systems, life cycles and movement understandable without familiar bones or limbs.
nodes.wonder: Can you predict the direction of the next pulse?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

nodes.summary: A bell-shaped jelly with long tentacles that carry stinging cells for capturing prey.
nodes.key_fact: A jelly's sting comes from microscopic capsules called nematocysts.
nodes.explainer: Touch triggers tiny harpoon-like structures that fire from specialised cells. The sting helps a slow-moving animal catch zooplankton and small prey.
nodes.why_it_matters: It shows how microscopic structures can act as a powerful feeding and defence system.
nodes.wonder: How fast must a microscopic harpoon fire to catch swimming prey?

nodes.summary: Its yellow centre and pale bell resemble a fried egg drifting through the water.
nodes.key_fact: The familiar name describes appearance, not a relationship to eggs.
nodes.explainer: Like other jellies, it alternates between attached polyp and free-swimming medusa stages during its life cycle.
nodes.why_it_matters: Changing body forms let one species use different habitats and feeding strategies across its life.
nodes.wonder: Why might one animal need two very different body plans?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

nodes.summary: A large freshwater fish that breathes mainly with gills but can gulp air using a single lung.
nodes.key_fact: Lungfish are closer evolutionary relatives of land vertebrates than most other living fishes are.
nodes.explainer: Its lobe-like fins and air-breathing anatomy help scientists compare living fishes with the ancestors of four-limbed vertebrates.
nodes.why_it_matters: The species helps explain the long evolutionary transition from fins and gills toward limbs and lungs.
nodes.wonder: Which came first in evolution: stronger fins or better air breathing?

nodes.summary: A giant South American freshwater fish that must surface regularly to breathe air.
nodes.key_fact: An Arapaima uses a highly vascularised swim bladder as an air-breathing organ.
nodes.explainer: Low-oxygen tropical waters reward animals able to use atmospheric oxygen. Surfacing solves one problem but exposes the fish to people and predators.
nodes.why_it_matters: Its physiology shows that water-dwelling vertebrates can evolve many ways to obtain oxygen.
nodes.wonder: How would you sleep if you had to keep returning to the surface?

nodes.summary: An ancient-looking coastal arthropod more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs.
nodes.key_fact: Copper-based hemocyanin makes horseshoe crab blood blue.
nodes.explainer: Book gills exchange gases, many eyes sense light, and the long tail helps the animal right itself. Its biomedical importance comes from blood cells that react strongly to bacterial contamination.
nodes.why_it_matters: Coastal habitat loss and harvesting connect this animal's survival to medicine and shoreline management.
nodes.wonder: How can an animal's immune system help keep human medicines safe?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

nodes.summary: A small bottom-dwelling shark that can 'walk' across reef flats using paired fins.
nodes.key_fact: It can tolerate periods of very low oxygen in shallow tide pools.
nodes.explainer: Strong pectoral and pelvic fins push the body over the bottom. Dark eye-spots may distract predators, while electroreception helps locate hidden prey.
nodes.why_it_matters: Its unusual movement and oxygen tolerance show how sharks diversified beyond constant open-water swimming.
nodes.wonder: When is walking better than swimming for a shark?

nodes.summary: A freshwater filter feeder whose long paddle-shaped snout detects tiny prey through electrical signals.
nodes.key_fact: Its filter-feeding gill rakers strain plankton from water as it swims.
nodes.explainer: The snout is packed with electroreceptors, helping the fish locate concentrations of zooplankton even when visibility is poor.
nodes.why_it_matters: Dams can block the long river journeys adults need to reach spawning grounds.
nodes.wonder: What would an electrical map of a river feel like?

nodes.summary: An aquatic salamander that keeps larval features such as external gills into adulthood.
nodes.key_fact: Axolotls can regenerate limbs and repair several other complex tissues.
nodes.explainer: Most salamanders metamorphose into a more terrestrial adult form. Axolotls usually remain aquatic and sexually mature without completing that transformation, a condition called neoteny.
nodes.why_it_matters: Wild Axolotls are critically endangered even though captive animals are common in laboratories and homes.
nodes.wonder: Why can an Axolotl regrow a limb when a human cannot?

nodes.summary: A small tropical frog whose bright colours can warn predators; the official page does not name the displayed species.
nodes.key_fact: Many poison frog toxins come from chemicals in their wild diet, so captive frogs may not be toxic.
nodes.explainer: Warning colouration works when predators learn or inherit an avoidance of conspicuous patterns. Different poison frog species vary greatly in colour and toxicity.
nodes.why_it_matters: Naming the exact species matters because conservation status, range and biology are not identical across the group.
nodes.wonder: Why advertise yourself brightly instead of hiding?

nodes.summary: A coastal fish famous for shooting jets of water at insects above the surface.
nodes.key_fact: Archerfish compensate for refraction when aiming through the water's surface.
nodes.explainer: The fish forms a narrow groove with its tongue and mouth, then squeezes water into an accelerating jet that knocks prey down.
nodes.why_it_matters: Its hunting shows sophisticated vision, learning and control in an animal with a very different brain from ours.
nodes.wonder: Where would you aim if the surface makes an insect appear in the wrong place?

nodes.summary: A fish that uses modified fins to skip over mud and moist skin and gills to manage time out of water.
nodes.key_fact: Its raised eyes can look above the mud while much of the body stays low and hidden.
nodes.explainer: Mudskippers keep breathing surfaces moist and use sturdy paired fins like crutches. Burrows provide shelter and more stable conditions during tidal change.
nodes.why_it_matters: Their survival depends on healthy mudflats and mangroves—habitats easily removed by coastal development.
nodes.wonder: Is a mudskipper a fish visiting land, or a land animal returning to water?

nodes.summary: A large Singapore sea star with bold dark knobs and hundreds of small tube feet beneath its arms.
nodes.key_fact: Sea stars are echinoderms, relatives of sea urchins and sea cucumbers—not fishes.
nodes.explainer: A water vascular system operates the tube feet for movement, attachment and handling food. The mouth is on the underside.
nodes.why_it_matters: Singapore's intertidal sea stars depend on seagrass, reef flats and careful behaviour around sensitive shores.
nodes.wonder: How can hundreds of tiny feet move one large body together?

nodes.summary: An upright-swimming fish that anchors its grasping tail to seagrass and other structures.
nodes.key_fact: In seahorses, the male carries developing embryos in a brood pouch and gives birth.
nodes.explainer: A tubular snout sucks in tiny prey, independently moving eyes scan the surroundings, and camouflage helps this weak swimmer avoid detection.
nodes.why_it_matters: Seahorses are vulnerable when seagrass and shallow coastal habitat are damaged.
nodes.wonder: Why might staying still be a better hunting strategy than chasing prey?

nodes.summary: A large shark with protruding teeth and a surprisingly slow, steady swimming style.
nodes.key_fact: It gulps air at the surface and stores it in the stomach to help maintain neutral buoyancy.
nodes.explainer: Air reduces the need to keep swimming for lift. Although its exposed teeth look fierce, appearance alone does not describe behaviour or risk.
nodes.why_it_matters: Very low reproductive output makes populations slow to recover from fishing pressure.
nodes.wonder: How does swallowed air help a shark hover?

nodes.summary: A wide-headed shark whose scalloped front edge gives the species its common name.
nodes.key_fact: The broad head spreads eyes and electroreceptors across a wider search area.
nodes.explainer: Wide-set eyes provide extensive visual coverage, while sensory pores help detect the electrical activity of prey, including animals hidden under sand.
nodes.why_it_matters: Scalloped Hammerheads are critically endangered, with schooling behaviour making many adults vulnerable at once.
nodes.wonder: What can a hammer-shaped head sense that a narrow head might miss?

nodes.summary: A coastal shark recognisable by its tall first dorsal fin and preference for continental shelf waters.
nodes.key_fact: Young Sandbar Sharks may use shallow coastal nursery areas.
nodes.explainer: A streamlined body supports steady cruising while electroreception, smell and hearing help locate fish and bottom-dwelling prey.
nodes.why_it_matters: Coastal habitat use brings this shark into frequent contact with fisheries and human activity.
nodes.wonder: Why are shallow nurseries useful for young sharks?

nodes.summary: A mostly nocturnal bottom-associated shark that rests in caves and uses strong suction to pull out prey.
nodes.key_fact: Powerful cheek muscles help it extract crabs, lobsters and fishes from reef crevices.
nodes.explainer: This carpet shark spends much of the day resting and becomes more active after dark. Small comb-like teeth crush hard-shelled prey.
nodes.why_it_matters: Coral reef damage removes both its shelter and feeding grounds.
nodes.wonder: Why might suction work better than biting inside a narrow crack?

nodes.summary: Colonies of tiny coral polyps create living structures that shelter an enormous variety of reef life.
nodes.key_fact: A coral reef is built by animals, often working in partnership with photosynthetic algae.
nodes.explainer: Hard corals deposit calcium carbonate skeletons. Soft corals usually lack massive stony skeletons. Each colony contains many connected polyps with tentacles.
nodes.why_it_matters: Heat stress can disrupt coral–algae partnerships and cause bleaching, weakening the habitat many species need.
nodes.wonder: How can animals smaller than a fingertip build a structure visible from space?

nodes.summary: A huge reef bivalve whose colourful mantle contains symbiotic algae.
nodes.key_fact: Giant clams gain nutrition both from filter feeding and from sugars made by partner algae.
nodes.explainer: The clam pumps water over its gills to collect particles. Light reaches algae in the exposed mantle, while iridescent cells help distribute that light.
nodes.why_it_matters: It links sunlight, plankton, water quality and animal–algae partnership in one visible organism.
nodes.wonder: Is the clam feeding from water, sunlight, or both?

nodes.summary: A long reef fish that hides in crevices; the official Coral Gardens page does not name the displayed species.
nodes.key_fact: Morays use a second set of jaws in the throat to help pull prey inward.
nodes.explainer: The eel-like body fits narrow spaces. Repeated mouth opening moves water over the gills and should not automatically be read as aggression.
nodes.why_it_matters: Precise species names matter because morays vary in size, range, diet and conservation needs.
nodes.wonder: How do you swallow prey when you cannot expand your head very far?

nodes.summary: A seahorse relative whose leaf-like appendages and swaying movement disguise it among seaweed.
nodes.key_fact: The decorative appendages are mainly camouflage; small transparent fins provide propulsion.
nodes.explainer: A long tube-like snout sucks in tiny crustaceans. Like seahorses, the male carries eggs, but they attach beneath the tail rather than inside a pouch.
nodes.why_it_matters: Camouflage specialists depend on the habitat background their bodies evolved to match.
nodes.wonder: Which parts are for swimming, and which are only for looking like seaweed?

nodes.summary: A reef fish with fused beak-like teeth and the ability to inflate its body when threatened.
nodes.key_fact: Inflation uses water to make the body suddenly larger and harder for a predator to swallow.
nodes.explainer: Strong teeth crush hard food. Slow swimming is balanced by defence: a tough inflated body and, in some puffers, powerful toxins.
nodes.why_it_matters: It demonstrates evolutionary trade-offs between speed, feeding equipment and defence.
nodes.wonder: Why spend energy swimming fast if you have another way to avoid being eaten?

nodes.summary: A small reef fish protected among a sea anemone's stinging tentacles.
nodes.key_fact: A specialised mucus coating helps prevent the host anemone from stinging the fish.
nodes.explainer: The fish gains shelter; the anemone can gain nutrients, cleaning, water movement and defence. The exact benefits vary among species and conditions.
nodes.why_it_matters: Their partnership makes both animals vulnerable when reefs and host anemones decline.
nodes.wonder: How can one animal's weapon become another animal's safe home?

nodes.summary: A weak-swimming seagrass resident that ambushes tiny prey with a fast suction-feeding snout.
nodes.key_fact: Male seahorses brood developing young and give birth.
nodes.explainer: A grasping tail anchors the body while independently moving eyes search for prey. Rapid head rotation and mouth expansion pull crustaceans inward.
nodes.why_it_matters: Habitat loss affects an animal that cannot simply outswim strong currents or travel easily to a new meadow.
nodes.wonder: How can a slow swimmer become a fast hunter?

visual.caption: Longsnout Seahorse — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A slender armoured fish that often swims vertically, head down, in tightly coordinated groups.
nodes.key_fact: Thin bony plates cover the body instead of ordinary fish scales.
nodes.explainer: Vertical posture and synchronised movement can help the fish disappear among coral branches or sea urchin spines. A tube-like mouth captures plankton.
nodes.why_it_matters: Its specialised shelter strategy ties survival closely to healthy reefs and seagrass beds.
nodes.wonder: Why might swimming the 'wrong' way up make you harder to see?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

visual.caption: Razorfish — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A striped ambush predator with broad fan-like fins and venomous dorsal spines.
nodes.key_fact: Venom is defensive; the fish hunts mainly by cornering and swallowing smaller animals.
nodes.explainer: Large pectoral fins help herd prey, while rapid mouth expansion creates suction. The conspicuous spines warn would-be predators.
nodes.why_it_matters: A species can be a valued native predator in one region and a damaging invasive predator in another.
nodes.wonder: How can the same animal belong in one reef and threaten another?

nodes.summary: A small deep-bodied fish with an elongated snout used to pick tiny prey from the water.
nodes.key_fact: Its narrow jaws create a precise tube for suction feeding.
nodes.explainer: Schools can reduce individual predation risk, while the body shape and snout suit life around reefs and deeper coastal water.
nodes.why_it_matters: Small fishes often connect plankton to larger predators in marine food webs.
nodes.wonder: When is a long narrow mouth better than a wide one?

visual.caption: Longspine Snipefish — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A nocturnal reef fish protected by large, strong scales that resemble overlapping armour.
nodes.key_fact: Large eyes help it gather light when it leaves shelter after dark.
nodes.explainer: During daylight it hides in reef crevices; at night it emerges to feed. Red colouration becomes less conspicuous as red light disappears with depth.
nodes.why_it_matters: Day and night create different ecological worlds on the same reef.
nodes.wonder: Why can bright red become good camouflage underwater?

nodes.summary: A grazing echinoderm whose very long movable spines provide defence and shelter for smaller animals.
nodes.key_fact: Five jaw-like structures form a feeding apparatus called Aristotle's lantern.
nodes.explainer: Tube feet move and grip while the mouth scrapes algae. Spines discourage predators and create a protected space around the body.
nodes.why_it_matters: Grazing can stop algae from overwhelming corals, but ecosystem imbalance can also produce damaging urchin outbreaks.
nodes.wonder: How can one grazer both help and harm a reef?

visual.caption: Long-spined Sea Urchin — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A very large reef fish whose fused teeth form a beak capable of biting hard coral surfaces.
nodes.key_fact: Its feeding breaks reef material into fine sediment and helps shape sandy habitats.
nodes.explainer: Powerful jaws scrape algae and coral material. Grinding plates farther back process each bite before digestion.
nodes.why_it_matters: Large reef grazers can strongly influence algae, coral competition and sediment production.
nodes.wonder: How much of a tropical beach may have passed through an animal?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

visual.caption: Green Humphead Parrotfish — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A giant filter-feeding ray; the official habitat page names manta rays without specifying the displayed species.
nodes.key_fact: Cephalic fins help funnel plankton-rich water toward the mouth.
nodes.explainer: Mantas swim by flapping broad pectoral fins like wings. They must find dense patches of tiny food despite their enormous size.
nodes.why_it_matters: Species-level identification is important because range and conservation assessments differ between manta species.
nodes.wonder: How can one of the ocean's largest fishes live on some of its smallest organisms?

nodes.summary: A spotted ray that appears to fly through open water while using broad tooth plates to crush prey.
nodes.key_fact: Its flattened teeth can crush molluscs and crustaceans hidden in the bottom.
nodes.explainer: A long snout helps investigate sediment, and electroreception helps locate buried animals. Powerful fins carry it between feeding areas.
nodes.why_it_matters: Coastal feeding habitats and open-water movement expose the ray to multiple human pressures.
nodes.wonder: How do you find a buried clam without seeing it?

visual.alt: Official profile photograph of Spotted Eagle Ray
visual.caption: Spotted Eagle Ray — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A bottom-associated carpet shark whose young have stripes while adults develop spots.
nodes.key_fact: The common name describes the striped juvenile pattern, not the spotted adult.
nodes.explainer: A flexible body and small barbels help the shark search reef crevices for molluscs, crustaceans and fishes, often at night.
nodes.why_it_matters: Changing appearance across life stages can cause the same species to be mistaken for two different animals.
nodes.wonder: Why might a young animal need different camouflage from an adult?

nodes.summary: One of the largest reef-associated bony fishes, with a cavernous mouth built for ambush and suction.
nodes.key_fact: Giant Groupers can reach roughly 2.7 metres and hundreds of kilograms.
nodes.explainer: A rapid expansion of the mouth pulls in fishes and crustaceans. Large adults occupy reefs, caves and wrecks where cover helps an ambush predator.
nodes.why_it_matters: Large, slow-growing reef predators are vulnerable to heavy fishing and habitat loss.
nodes.wonder: How can a fish catch prey without chasing it very far?

visual.alt: Official profile photograph of Giant Grouper
visual.caption: Giant Grouper — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A huge, colourful reef fish with a forehead hump and strong jaws for hard-shelled prey.
nodes.key_fact: It can eat crown-of-thorns sea stars, which prey on corals.
nodes.explainer: Fused front teeth and crushing throat teeth process molluscs, crustaceans and echinoderms. Adults can change sex from female to male.
nodes.why_it_matters: The species is endangered because slow reproduction, reef damage and fishing make populations difficult to rebuild.
nodes.wonder: How can one predator help protect the structure of an entire reef?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

nodes.summary: A silvery coastal fish able to gulp air, helping it tolerate warm or oxygen-poor water.
nodes.key_fact: A modified swim bladder can act as a breathing organ.
nodes.explainer: Tarpon move between coastal, estuarine and freshwater environments. Air breathing gives them access to habitats that exclude less tolerant fishes.
nodes.why_it_matters: Animals moving among habitats depend on the connections between them, not just one protected site.
nodes.wonder: When does breathing air give a fish an advantage?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

nodes.summary: A small ambush predator whose colour, frilly outline and grasping fins mimic floating Sargassum seaweed.
nodes.key_fact: It can use modified pectoral fins to clamber through the floating weed.
nodes.explainer: Camouflage hides the fish from both predators and prey. A rapidly expanding mouth can swallow surprisingly large animals at close range.
nodes.why_it_matters: Its entire lifestyle depends on a mobile habitat created by floating algae.
nodes.wonder: How do you tell the animal from the habitat?

nodes.summary: Tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that gather in swarms and feed many fishes.
nodes.key_fact: Mysids are not true shrimps, although their body shape looks similar.
nodes.explainer: They filter or pick small particles and plankton, then transfer that energy to larger predators. Females carry young in a brood pouch.
nodes.why_it_matters: Small prey animals can be the hidden bridge between microscopic production and visible fishes.
nodes.wonder: Would an ocean food web work without tiny animals in the middle?

nodes.summary: A fish with oversized eyes suited to finding prey where light is limited.
nodes.key_fact: Large eyes collect more available light but require more head space and energy.
nodes.explainer: Bigeyes commonly shelter by day and feed more actively in dim conditions, using vision to locate crustaceans and small fishes.
nodes.why_it_matters: Eye size illustrates an evolutionary trade-off shaped by depth and time of activity.
nodes.wonder: How large would your eyes need to be if twilight never ended?

nodes.summary: A heavily armoured nocturnal fish with light-producing bacteria near its lower jaw.
nodes.key_fact: Its glow is produced by symbiotic bacteria housed in specialised organs.
nodes.explainer: The fish can partly cover the light organs. Bioluminescence may help it communicate, find prey or reduce its silhouette in dim water.
nodes.why_it_matters: A partnership with microbes gives the fish a capability neither partner would express in the same way alone.
nodes.wonder: Would you use a living light to signal, hunt or hide?

nodes.summary: A social coastal dolphin that uses whistles, clicks, learning and cooperation to navigate its world.
nodes.key_fact: Echolocation clicks return echoes that reveal an object's distance, size, shape and material clues.
nodes.explainer: Dolphins breathe air, nurse their young and maintain complex social relationships. Their brains integrate sound, memory and learned behaviour.
nodes.why_it_matters: The species is near threatened and depends on coastal waters affected by fishing, noise, pollution and habitat change.
nodes.wonder: What would an object look like if you could only 'see' it through echoes?

visual.caption: Indo-Pacific Bottlenose Dolphin — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A large eel-shaped reef fish that appears green because yellowish mucus overlays blue-grey skin.
nodes.key_fact: A second set of jaws in the throat moves forward to help grasp and transport prey.
nodes.explainer: The flexible body enters crevices where most large predators cannot follow. Smell is especially important when hunting in dim shelter.
nodes.why_it_matters: The animal's colour and open-mouth breathing are easy to misinterpret without looking closer.
nodes.wonder: Why might a predator need two sets of jaws?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

visual.alt: Official profile photograph of Green Moray
visual.caption: Green Moray — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: One of the world's heaviest crabs, built for a cold-water life on the seafloor.
nodes.key_fact: A large claw can be much bigger than the other and is used for crushing food.
nodes.explainer: The heavy exoskeleton protects the body, while jointed legs carry the crab over the bottom. Like other crustaceans it must moult to grow.
nodes.why_it_matters: Slow-growing deep and cold-water animals may be especially vulnerable to harvesting.
nodes.wonder: How does an animal stay safe while its new shell is still soft?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — official A–Z animal page

nodes.summary: A small striped reef fish from a tiny natural range, often sheltering among sea urchin spines.
nodes.key_fact: The male carries fertilised eggs and newly hatched young in his mouth.
nodes.explainer: Mouthbrooding protects a small number of relatively well-developed young. Limited dispersal keeps populations local and genetically structured.
nodes.why_it_matters: A very restricted range and aquarium trade collection have contributed to endangered status.
nodes.wonder: How does a parent eat while carrying young in its mouth?

nodes.summary: A bright reef grazer with a sharp defensive spine on each side of the tail base.
nodes.key_fact: Its constant grazing helps remove algae from reef surfaces.
nodes.explainer: A small mouth clips plant material, while the laterally compressed body turns quickly among reef structures. The tail spine can deter attack.
nodes.why_it_matters: Herbivorous fishes help maintain the balance between algae and reef-building organisms.
nodes.wonder: What happens to a reef when too many grazers disappear?

nodes.summary: A slender spotted carpet shark also widely called the Zebra Shark; names can vary by region and life stage.
nodes.key_fact: Juveniles are dark with pale bands, while adults are pale with dark spots.
nodes.explainer: The official Artificial Habitats page uses 'Indo-Pacific Leopard Shark.' This globe keeps the visitor-page name while showing its connection to the Zebra Shark entry.
nodes.why_it_matters: Common names can create accidental duplicates, so scientific identification is essential in a complete animal catalogue.
nodes.wonder: When do two names describe one species rather than two animals?

visual.alt: Official profile photograph of Indo-Pacific Leopard Shark
visual.caption: Indo-Pacific Leopard Shark — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A broad bottom-associated ray with a rounded disc and spotted or blotched upper surface.
nodes.key_fact: Spiracles behind the eyes draw water toward the gills while the ray rests on the bottom.
nodes.explainer: Camouflage hides the ray against sand and rubble. Electroreception helps it locate buried molluscs, crustaceans and fishes.
nodes.why_it_matters: Bottom trawling and coastal habitat damage can affect animals that feed and rest on the seabed.
nodes.wonder: How can a flat animal breathe while buried in sand?

nodes.summary: A small hammerhead relative with a smooth, shovel-shaped head.
nodes.key_fact: Bonnetheads eat crustaceans and fishes and can also digest substantial seagrass material.
nodes.explainer: The head carries widely distributed sensory organs, while a compact body manoeuvres through shallow coastal habitat.
nodes.why_it_matters: Its flexible diet challenges the simple idea that every shark is strictly carnivorous.
nodes.wonder: Can an animal be both a shark and partly omnivorous?

visual.caption: Bonnethead Shark — official Animals A–Z profile

nodes.summary: A deep-sea crustacean with overlapping body plates and many jointed legs.
nodes.key_fact: Isopods are crustacean relatives of familiar woodlice and pill bugs.
nodes.explainer: Armour protects the body, while a scavenging lifestyle helps exploit unpredictable food reaching the deep seafloor.
nodes.why_it_matters: Scavengers recycle rare food and move nutrients through an ecosystem where little is wasted.
nodes.wonder: How long would you wait between meals if food almost never arrived?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — Whale Fall and Seamount

nodes.summary: A red deep-water crustacean adapted to cold, dim environments near the seafloor.
nodes.key_fact: Red wavelengths disappear quickly underwater, so a red animal can look dark in deep blue light.
nodes.explainer: Long antennae sense the surroundings beyond the reach of vision, while legs and mouthparts search for small food items on or near the bottom.
nodes.why_it_matters: Colour only functions in relation to the light available in an animal's habitat.
nodes.wonder: Can a bright red animal be camouflaged?

sources.title: Singapore Oceanarium — Whale Fall and Seamount

nodes.summary: A deep-water cartilaginous fish related to sharks and rays but belonging to the separate chimaera lineage.
nodes.key_fact: Tooth plates crush hard prey and keep growing as they wear.
nodes.explainer: Large eyes, electroreception and a sensory lateral-line system help the fish operate in dim water. A venomous dorsal spine provides defence.
nodes.why_it_matters: Chimaeras reveal a distinct branch of cartilaginous-fish evolution often overshadowed by sharks.
nodes.wonder: Which senses become most useful when sunlight disappears?

Large eyes and light-related adaptations suit dim habitats.
